messages.content: What is the cardiovascular system and how does the heart work?

The cardiovascular system (circulatory system) consists of the heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries), and blood, working together to deliver oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and immune cells to tissues and remove metabolic waste products (CO₂, urea). The heart: a four-chambered muscular pump located in the mediastinum, slightly left of centre. Anatomy: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle. The interventricular septum separates the left and right sides. Valves (prevent backflow): atrioventricular valves (tricuspid — right, mitral/bicuspid — left) between atria and ventricles; semilunar valves (pulmonary — right ventricular outflow, aortic — left ventricular outflow) between ventricles and great arteries. Cardiac cycle: Diastole — ventricles relax and fill with blood from the atria. Systole — ventricles contract and eject blood. Phases: isovolumetric contraction (both AV and semilunar valves closed; pressure rises without volume change) → ejection (semilunar valves open; blood ejected into pulmonary artery/aorta) → isovolumetric relaxation → filling. Heart sounds: S1 ('lub') = AV valve closure; S2 ('dub') = semilunar valve closure. Circulation: pulmonary circulation (right heart → pulmonary arteries → lungs [oxygenation] → pulmonary veins → left heart) and systemic circulation (left heart → aorta → systemic arteries → capillary beds [O₂/nutrient exchange] → veins → right heart). Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (typically 70ml × 70bpm = ~5L/min at rest; can increase to ~25L/min during maximal exercise). Electrical conduction: SA node (pacemaker) → AV node → Bundle of His → Purkinje fibres → ventricular contraction. Electrocardiogram (ECG) records electrical activity — P wave (atrial depolarisation), QRS complex (ventricular depolarisation), T wave (ventricular repolarisation).
What is hypertension and what are its complications?

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is the most common cardiovascular condition globally, affecting approximately 1.28 billion adults worldwide (WHO, 2021). Blood pressure (BP) is the force exerted by blood on arterial walls, measured in mmHg as systolic/diastolic. Normal BP: <120/<80 mmHg. Elevated: 120-129/<80. Stage 1 hypertension: 130-139/80-89. Stage 2: ≥140/≥90. Hypertensive crisis: >180/>120 (requires emergency treatment). Classification: Primary (essential) hypertension (~90-95% of cases): no identifiable single cause; results from a complex interaction of genetic, lifestyle, and environmental factors — excess sodium intake (upregulates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system), obesity, physical inactivity, alcohol, stress, ageing (loss of arterial elasticity), and genetic predisposition. Secondary hypertension (~5-10%): caused by an identifiable condition — renal artery stenosis (most common secondary cause), chronic kidney disease, primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), phaeochromocytoma, obstructive sleep apnoea, thyroid disorders, certain medications (NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, decongestants). The 'silent killer': hypertension typically produces no symptoms for decades — hence massive underdiagnosis and undertreament globally. Damage accumulates insidiously. Complications (target organ damage): (1) Cardiovascular: coronary artery disease, left ventricular hypertrophy (hypertension is the major modifiable risk factor for heart failure), myocardial infarction. (2) Cerebrovascular: haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke (hypertension is the single most important modifiable stroke risk factor); hypertensive encephalopathy. (3) Renal: hypertensive nephropathy → chronic kidney disease → end-stage renal disease (and CKD itself worsens hypertension — a vicious cycle). (4) Retinal: hypertensive retinopathy; papilloedema in severe hypertension.
What is diabetes mellitus and what are the differences between type 1 and type 2?

Diabetes mellitus is a metabolic disorder characterised by chronic hyperglycaemia (high blood glucose) resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. Glucose is the primary cellular fuel; insulin (produced by pancreatic beta cells) is required for most cells to take up glucose. Without adequate insulin action, glucose accumulates in the blood while cells are starved. Diagnosis: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL), or 2-hour glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L during an OGTT, or HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%), or random glucose ≥11.1 with symptoms. Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM, ~5-10% of cases): autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells — T-cell mediated immune attack, with autoantibodies against insulin (IAA), GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8. Results in absolute insulin deficiency. Onset: typically childhood or adolescence (but can occur at any age). Presentation: rapid onset, often with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA — life-threatening hyperglycaemic emergency: glucose >11, ketones, acidosis). Treatment: lifelong insulin replacement (multiple daily injections or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion — 'insulin pump'). Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM, ~90-95% of cases): progressive insulin resistance (peripheral tissues — muscle, liver, adipose — respond inadequately to insulin) combined with progressive beta-cell failure (beta cells cannot compensate by secreting more insulin). Risk factors: obesity (particularly visceral/central adiposity), physical inactivity, age, family history, gestational diabetes, ethnicity (South Asian, Black African, Hispanic populations have higher risk). Onset: typically gradual, often asymptomatic for years (the 'silent' phase). Treatment: lifestyle modifications (diet, exercise — the most effective intervention); metformin (first-line pharmacotherapy — reduces hepatic glucose output); GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors (significant CV and renal protective effects); sulphonylureas; insulin if oral agents insufficient.
What is cancer and what are the hallmarks of cancer biology?

Cancer is a group of diseases characterised by uncontrolled cell proliferation, invasion of surrounding tissues, and potential metastasis (spread to distant sites via blood or lymphatics). It arises from the accumulation of somatic mutations in genes regulating cell division, apoptosis, and other cellular processes. Hanahan and Weinberg's 'Hallmarks of Cancer' (2000, revised 2011 and 2022) provides the conceptual framework: (1) Sustaining proliferative signalling: cancer cells produce their own growth signals (autocrine signalling) or become hypersensitive to growth factors. Oncogene activation (RAS mutation in 30% of cancers). (2) Evading growth suppressors: inactivation of tumour suppressor genes (RB, TP53 — 'guardian of the genome'; BRCA1/2). (3) Resisting cell death: upregulation of anti-apoptotic proteins (BCL-2), loss of TP53 — evading programmed cell death. (4) Enabling replicative immortality: telomere maintenance (telomerase — present in 90% of cancers; normally repressed in adult somatic cells — prevents 'telomere erosion crisis' that limits normal cell replication). (5) Inducing angiogenesis: tumours require new blood vessel growth (VEGF secretion) beyond ~1-2mm³. (6) Activating invasion and metastasis: loss of E-cadherin, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), matrix metalloprotease secretion. (7) Deregulating cellular energetics: the Warburg effect — cancer cells preferentially use aerobic glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen (generating lactic acid) — provides biosynthetic precursors for rapid growth. (8) Avoiding immune destruction: PD-L1 expression (targeted by immunotherapy — checkpoint inhibitors: pembrolizumab, nivolumab). (9) Tumour-promoting inflammation: tumour microenvironment contains immunosuppressive cells (regulatory T cells, M2 macrophages). (10) Genomic instability: increased mutation rate due to DNA repair defects (microsatellite instability — Lynch syndrome; chromosomal instability).
What is antibiotic resistance and why is it a global health crisis?

Antibiotic resistance (antimicrobial resistance, AMR) occurs when bacteria evolve mechanisms to survive exposure to antibiotics that would normally kill them or halt their growth. It is one of the greatest threats to global health, food security, and development. WHO estimates that AMR currently causes ~700,000 deaths annually; without action, this could rise to 10 million per year by 2050 (exceeding cancer deaths). Mechanisms of resistance: (1) Enzymatic drug inactivation: beta-lactamases cleave the beta-lactam ring of penicillins and cephalosporins, rendering them inactive (Extended Spectrum Beta-Lactamases — ESBLs; carbapenemases — NDM-1, KPC). (2) Target modification: mutations alter the antibiotic's target so the drug cannot bind. Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) produces a modified penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for all beta-lactams. (3) Efflux pumps: bacteria actively pump antibiotics out of the cell before they can act. (4) Reduced permeability: loss of outer membrane porins in Gram-negative bacteria reduces antibiotic entry. (5) Bypass mechanisms: MRSA example above also uses an alternative pathway. Genetic transmission: resistance genes spread not only through bacterial reproduction (vertical transmission) but through horizontal gene transfer — plasmids, transposons, and bacteriophages carrying resistance genes can jump between species (enabling one resistant strain to spread resistance broadly). Drivers: (1) Overuse and misuse in human medicine (prescribing antibiotics for viral infections; not completing courses). (2) Massive agricultural use (~70% of antibiotics used globally are in livestock — for growth promotion and disease prevention in crowded conditions). (3) Environmental contamination (pharmaceutical manufacturing waste — Indian rivers with extraordinarily high antibiotic concentrations). Solutions: new antibiotic development (no new antibiotic class reached the market between 1987-2017); phage therapy; antibiotic stewardship programmes; One Health approach (human, animal, environmental health integrated).
What is the immune response to vaccines and how do vaccines work?

Vaccines are biological preparations that provide active, adaptive immunity against infectious diseases without causing the disease itself. They train the immune system to recognise and respond rapidly to specific pathogens. Immunological basis: upon first exposure to a pathogen or vaccine antigen, the adaptive immune response takes 1-2 weeks to develop (primary response): B cells specific to the antigen are clonally selected, proliferate, differentiate into plasma cells (secreting antibodies) and memory B cells. T helper cells (CD4+) activate B cells and coordinate the response; cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) kill infected cells. Memory B and T cells persist for years to decades. On re-exposure (or booster vaccination), the memory response is faster (within days) and produces more antibodies at higher titre — the secondary (anamnestic) response. This explains why vaccinated individuals are protected: when they encounter the actual pathogen, their pre-existing memory cells generate a rapid, strong response before the pathogen can cause serious disease. Types of vaccines: (1) Live attenuated: weakened (attenuated) but replication-competent pathogen (MMR, varicella, yellow fever). Produces strongest, longest-lasting immunity (closely mimics natural infection). Contraindicated in immunocompromised patients. (2) Inactivated: killed pathogen (influenza, hepatitis A, polio — Salk). Safer, but typically requires adjuvants and boosters. (3) Subunit/protein: specific pathogen proteins (hepatitis B surface antigen, HPV capsid proteins — VLPs, pertussis toxoid). Very safe; may need adjuvants. (4) mRNA vaccines: (Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2, Moderna mRNA-1273 — COVID-19): mRNA encoding the spike protein → cells produce spike protein → immune response → memory. No DNA is involved; mRNA is rapidly degraded. Rapid platform development is the major advantage. (5) Viral vector: (AstraZeneca ChAdOx1, Janssen Ad26.COV2.S): adenoviral vector delivers DNA encoding spike protein. Herd immunity: when sufficient proportion of a population is immune (through vaccination or prior infection), transmission chains break → protection of unvaccinated individuals. Threshold depends on R₀ (basic reproduction number): measles (R₀≈12-18) requires ~92-95% immunity; COVID (R₀≈5-6 for Delta) ~70-80%.
What is mental health and what are evidence-based treatments for depression?

Mental health is a state of psychological wellbeing in which an individual can realise their own potential, cope with the normal stresses of life, work productively, and contribute to their community (WHO). Mental disorders are clinically significant patterns of cognition, emotion, or behaviour associated with distress, disability, or risk of harm. Depression (Major Depressive Disorder, MDD): one of the most prevalent mental health conditions globally — affecting ~5% of the world population (WHO). Characterised by persistent depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure (anhedonia) for ≥2 weeks, plus ≥4 of: significant weight change, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, difficulty concentrating, recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation. Neurobiological basis: complex and not fully understood. Monoamine deficiency hypothesis: reduced serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine. Neuroplasticity hypothesis: reduced BDNF and hippocampal neurogenesis (stress-induced atrophy). HPA axis dysregulation: elevated cortisol in depression. Neuroinflammation: elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in a subset of patients. Evidence-based treatments: (1) Pharmacotherapy: SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors — fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram): first-line; well-tolerated; 4-6 weeks for effect. SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine): second-line or for anxiety-depression comorbidity. Mirtazapine, bupropion (NDRI). TCA, MAOI: older classes, effective but more side effects. Ketamine/esketamine (Spravato): rapid-acting NMDA antagonist for treatment-resistant depression — dissociative effects, abuse potential, monitored administration. (2) Psychotherapy: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) — identifying and restructuring negative automatic thoughts; comparable efficacy to antidepressants for mild-moderate depression. Behavioural Activation, Interpersonal Therapy (IPT), Psychodynamic therapy. (3) Combined: medication + therapy superior to either alone for severe depression. (4) Physical: regular aerobic exercise (30min, 3×/week) has demonstrated antidepressant efficacy. (5) ECT (electroconvulsive therapy): most effective treatment for severe/treatment-resistant depression; stigmatised but evidence-based.
What is surgery and what are the major types?

Surgery is the branch of medicine that treats disease, injury, or deformity by direct physical intervention — typically involving incision, manipulation, and/or repair of body structures. History: surgical practice predates recorded history (trepanation skulls from 10,000 BCE). Modern surgery was transformed by anaesthesia (ether 1846, chloroform 1847) and antiseptic technique (Lister 1867 — carbolic acid, building on Pasteur's germ theory). Major categories: (1) General surgery: operations on the abdominal organs — appendicectomy, cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal), bowel resection (colorectal cancer, Crohn's disease), hernia repair, gastric bypass (bariatric surgery). (2) Cardiac surgery: coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) — revascularisation using saphenous vein or internal mammary artery; valve repair/replacement; repair of congenital heart defects; heart transplantation. (3) Neurosurgery: craniotomy (brain tumour resection), aneurysm clipping, spinal surgery (discectomy, spinal fusion), deep brain stimulation (Parkinson's). (4) Orthopaedic surgery: fracture fixation, total joint arthroplasty (hip/knee replacement — one of the most successful operations in medicine), ligament reconstruction (ACL repair), spinal surgery. (5) Obstetrics/gynaecology: caesarean section, hysterectomy, laparoscopic procedures (endometriosis). (6) Transplant surgery: kidney, liver, heart, lung, pancreas, small bowel transplantation. Minimally invasive surgery: laparoscopy (multiple small incisions, camera, instruments — smaller wounds, faster recovery, less pain) and robotic surgery (da Vinci system — enhances dexterity and precision). Principles of safe surgery: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (sign-in, time-out, sign-out) — reduces surgical mortality and complications.
What is the opioid epidemic and how did it arise?

The opioid epidemic is a public health crisis, particularly severe in the United States, characterised by widespread addiction to and overdose deaths from opioid drugs — both prescription opioids and illicit heroin/fentanyl. Statistics: in the US, over 80,000 opioid overdose deaths occurred in 2021 (a record); since 1999, more than 500,000 Americans have died from opioid overdose. Origins and phases: Wave 1 (1990s-2000s): the crisis began with the dramatic increase in prescription opioids. Purdue Pharma's aggressive marketing of OxyContin (sustained-release oxycodone) from 1996, falsely claiming it had a low addiction potential due to its slow-release formulation. Marketing targeted primary care physicians, emphasising chronic pain management. Simultaneously, pain management advocacy promoted the 'fifth vital sign' movement (pain should be regularly assessed and aggressively treated) — inadvertently normalising opioid prescription. Physicians trained in inadequate pain management became over-reliant on opioids. 'Pill mills' (clinics prescribing large quantities without adequate assessment). Wave 2 (2010s): as prescription opioid supplies were tightened (stricter regulations, prescription drug monitoring programmes), many patients dependent on prescription opioids switched to cheaper, more accessible heroin. Overdose deaths from heroin rose sharply. Wave 3 (2013-present): illicitly manufactured fentanyl (100× more potent than morphine) and its analogues (carfentanil — 10,000× more potent) entered the drug supply, often mixed with or substituted for heroin. Small dosing errors are lethal. Fentanyl overdose deaths dominate current statistics. Pathophysiology: opioids act on μ-opioid receptors — produce analgesia, euphoria, and respiratory depression (mechanism of overdose death). Tolerance develops rapidly; withdrawal is intensely dysphoric. MOUD (Medications for Opioid Use Disorder): buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone), methadone, naltrexone are evidence-based treatments. Naloxone (Narcan) reversal saves lives.
What is epidemiology and how is it used in public health?

Epidemiology is the study of the distribution, determinants, and determinants of health and disease in populations — the science underlying public health decision-making. It answers: Who gets a disease? Where? When? Why? And how can we prevent it? Core measures: Incidence: the rate of new cases in a defined population over a specified time period — measures the risk of developing a disease. Prevalence: the proportion of a population with a disease at a given point in time (point prevalence) or during a period (period prevalence) — measures the burden of disease. Mortality rate: deaths per 100,000 per year. Case fatality rate (CFR): proportion of those with disease who die. Study designs: Descriptive: describe the distribution of disease by person, place, and time — generates hypotheses. Analytical: test hypotheses about risk factors. Cross-sectional ('snapshot'): measures exposure and outcome simultaneously; quick and cheap but cannot establish temporality (cause vs. effect ambiguous). Case-control: starts with cases (those with disease) and controls (without), looks backward at exposure. Efficient for rare diseases; subject to recall bias. Cohort: follows a population over time; compares those exposed vs. unexposed; establishes temporality; expensive and slow for rare diseases. Relative risk (RR): risk in exposed / risk in unexposed (cohort studies). Odds ratio (OR): odds of exposure in cases / odds of exposure in controls (case-control studies). Both measures quantify associations between exposures and outcomes. Confounding: a variable that is associated with both the exposure and outcome, distorting the observed association. Controlled by: study design (restriction, matching) and analysis (stratification, multivariable regression). Interventions: randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for evaluating treatments — randomisation eliminates confounding. Meta-analysis: combines results from multiple studies, increasing statistical power.
How do vaccines work and why do some people have concerns?

VACCINES — Training the Immune System

HOW THEY WORK:
Immune system must "see" a pathogen to build memory against it.
Vaccines: safely expose the immune system to antigen (part of pathogen) without causing disease.
First exposure (vaccination): slow primary response, 1-2 weeks.
Second exposure (actual infection or booster): rapid memory response, 1-3 days, much stronger.
The pathogen is cleared before symptoms can develop.

TYPES OF VACCINES:
Live attenuated: weakened pathogen still replicates. Strongest immunity. MMR, chickenpox, yellow fever.
 Risk: very rarely can revert (oral polio vaccine). Cannot give to immunocompromised.
Inactivated: killed pathogen. Safer. Flu shot, hepatitis A, polio (injected).
 Often needs boosters (weaker immune response than live).
Subunit/protein: just one or more proteins from pathogen. HPV, hepatitis B, pertussis component.
 Safest. No live pathogen at all.
mRNA: instructions to make pathogen protein. COVID-19 Pfizer, Moderna.
 mRNA never enters nucleus, cannot affect DNA. Degraded in days.
 Advantages: can be developed rapidly, highly effective.
Viral vector: adenovirus delivers instructions. AstraZeneca COVID, Johnson & Johnson.
Toxoid: inactivated toxin. Tetanus, diphtheria. Target the toxin not the bacteria.

HERD IMMUNITY:
When enough people immune, pathogen can''t spread even to unvaccinated.
Threshold: measles 95% (R0=15), COVID ~70-80%, flu ~50%.
Protects: infants too young to vaccinate, immunocompromised who can''t receive vaccines.

COMMON CONCERNS (honest discussion):
"Causes autism": 1998 Wakefield study — fraudulent, retracted, Wakefield lost medical licence.
23 studies involving 1.2 million children found no link. Science settled.
"Too many too soon": immune system handles millions of antigens daily. Vaccine antigens: tiny fraction.
"Natural immunity better": sometimes, but at cost of actually getting disease.
Side effects: injection site pain, low fever, fatigue — normal immune response. Serious adverse events: very rare (anaphylaxis ~1-2 per million doses).
Speed of COVID vaccine development: built on decades of mRNA and coronavirus research. Phases ran simultaneously (parallel rather than sequential), not skipped.
Explain cancer — what causes it and how is it treated?

CANCER — Uncontrolled Cell Growth

WHAT IS CANCER?
Normal cells: divide under tight control, respond to growth signals, undergo apoptosis (programmed death) when needed.
Cancer cells: ignore growth signals, grow uncontrollably, evade death signals, can invade other tissues (metastasis).

CAUSES — mutations in genes controlling cell division:
Proto-oncogenes: promote cell growth. Mutations -> oncogenes. Stuck in "always on."
 KRAS: most commonly mutated oncogene. Pancreatic, colorectal, lung cancers.
Tumour suppressor genes: brake pedals. Inactivation removes brakes.
 TP53: "guardian of the genome." Mutated in >50% of all cancers.
 BRCA1/2: hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

WHAT CAUSES MUTATIONS:
Replication errors: DNA copying mistakes (~3 per cell division). Mostly repaired.
Carcinogens: tobacco smoke (PAHs, nitrosamines), UV radiation, aflatoxin, alcohol, asbestos.
Viruses: HPV -> cervical, head/neck cancer. Hepatitis B/C -> liver cancer. Helicobacter pylori -> stomach.
Radiation: ionising radiation (X-rays, nuclear fallout) damages DNA directly.
Hereditary: BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome (colorectal). Increased risk but not deterministic.

HALLMARKS OF CANCER (Hanahan & Weinberg):
Self-sufficient growth signals. Evade anti-growth signals. Avoid apoptosis.
Limitless replication (telomerase). Angiogenesis (blood supply). Invasion/metastasis.
Immune evasion. Metabolic reprogramming (Warburg effect).

TREATMENTS:
Surgery: remove tumour. Curative if caught early and localised.
Radiation: high-energy X-rays damage tumour DNA. Stereotactic radiosurgery very precise.
Chemotherapy: cytotoxic drugs kill rapidly dividing cells. Affects hair, gut (rapidly dividing) — hence side effects.
Targeted therapy: drugs targeting specific mutations. Imatinib (Gleevec) for BCR-ABL in CML. Revolutionary.
Immunotherapy: unleash immune system. Checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab). PD-1/PD-L1 blockade.
 Cancer cells express PD-L1 to suppress immune response. Drug blocks this. Immune attacks cancer.
 Works for: melanoma, lung, bladder. Some achieve durable remission.
CAR-T cell therapy: genetically engineer patient''s T cells to target cancer. Leukaemia responses impressive.
Hormone therapy: ER+ breast cancer, prostate cancer dependent on testosterone.
How do drugs work — pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics?

PHARMACOLOGY — How Drugs Work in the Body

PHARMACODYNAMICS — what the drug does to the body.
Receptors: proteins that bind molecules and trigger cellular responses.
Drug binds receptor -> changes receptor activity -> biological effect.

Agonist: binds receptor, activates it (mimics natural molecule).
 Morphine: agonist at opioid receptors. Mimics endorphins. Pain relief + euphoria.
Antagonist: binds receptor, blocks it (no activation, blocks natural molecule).
 Beta-blockers (propranolol): block beta-adrenergic receptors. Slow heart rate, lower BP.
 Naloxone (Narcan): opioid antagonist. Reverses overdose by blocking opioid receptors.
Partial agonist: activates receptor but less than full agonist. Buprenorphine for opioid addiction.

Dose-response curve: as dose increases, effect increases until maximum (plateau).
EC50: dose producing 50% of maximum effect. Measure of potency.
Therapeutic index: ratio of toxic dose to therapeutic dose. Wide = safer drug.
 Penicillin: very wide. Lithium: very narrow (monitor blood levels).

PHARMACOKINETICS — what the body does to the drug.
ADME: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion.

Absorption: drug enters bloodstream. Oral -> gut absorption. IV -> 100% bioavailability.
 First-pass effect: oral drugs metabolised in liver before reaching circulation.
 Some drugs destroyed by stomach acid -> must give by injection.

Distribution: drug reaches tissues. Lipid-soluble: crosses blood-brain barrier, stored in fat.
 Protein binding: drug bound to albumin can''t act. Only free drug is active.

Metabolism: mostly liver (cytochrome P450 enzymes). Often inactivates drug (sometimes activates: prodrug).
 Drug interactions: one drug can inhibit or induce CYP enzymes affecting another drug''s levels.
 Codeine: prodrug converted to morphine by CYP2D6. Poor metabolisers: no effect. Rapid metabolisers: toxicity.

Excretion: kidneys (urine), bile (faeces), lungs (exhaled), sweat. Half-life: time to halve blood concentration.
 Short half-life (aspirin ~4h): dose multiple times daily. Long half-life (fluoxetine ~4 days): once daily.
 Renal failure: drugs excreted by kidneys accumulate. Dose adjustment needed.
